National Urogynecology & Pelvic Reconstructive Surgery (URPS) Workforce Microsimulation: 10-Year Projections & Empirical Audit (2025–2035)

URPS Microsimulation Research Group

2026-08-21

Executive Summary

This Results Report presents the 10-year empirical-hybrid projections of the Urogynecology and Pelvic Reconstructive Surgery (URPS) national workforce microsimulation model (urpssim). Combining multi-source empirical evidence—including CMS Part B provider-service tables (2013–2024), NPPES temporal provider registries, CMS Doctors & Clinicians data, UHC transparency-in-coverage negotiated rates, and ACGME fellowship case logs—with a dynamic multi-state female population model, the simulation tracks patient demand, workforce supply, care-seeking conversion, and spatial access across all 306 Dartmouth Hospital Referral Regions (HRRs).

Key findings include: - Widening National Supply Deficit: Under current fellowship training rates (55–64 certified graduates per year) and age/sex-specific career retirement hazards, active physician clinical FTE declines relative to female population growth, expanding the national clinical FTE gap from 3,851.8 FTEs in 2025 to 4,480.8 FTEs by 2035. - Patient-Flow Conservation Audit: Unmet or delayed patient demand grows from 2.07 million cases in 2025 to 2.95 million cases in 2035, as national appointment capacity fails to keep pace with demographic aging and PFD incidence. - Severe Geographic Maldistribution: 100% of the 306 HRRs experience a clinical FTE shortage exceeding 20% of required local demand throughout the 2025–2035 projection window. - Latent Access Adequacy (\(\theta_g\)): Bayesian latent factor calibration reveals a national average access score of 47.6% (95% CI: 41.2%–54.0%), with substantial cross-county variation driven by mystery-caller listing rates and appointment wait times.

1. Variable Definitions & Data Dictionary

To ensure complete clarity and transparency across all report tables, equations, and figures, the core simulation variables are defined below:

Demographic & Epidemiological Variables

  • Female Population (population / Female Pop (M)): Total estimated U.S. community-dwelling adult female population aged 18 and older, derived from U.S. Census Bureau ACS 5-year tract projections.
  • Incident Cases (incident_cases): Newly diagnosed pelvic floor disorder cases (SUI, UUI, POP Stage I–IV, FI, OAB) originating within the current calendar year.
  • Prevalent Cases (prevalent_cases / Prevalent PFD (M)): Total active pool of adult women living with one or more symptomatic pelvic floor disorders in year \(t\).

Care Cascade & Patient-Flow Variables

  • Care-Seeking Patients (care_seeking_n / Care Seeking (M)): Subset of prevalent women who actively present to the healthcare system for medical or surgical evaluation (\(\text{Care Seeking} = \text{Prevalent Cases} \times P(\text{care seeking} \mid \text{severity, insurance})\)).
  • Referred Patients (referred_n): Care-seeking patients who receive a formal subspecialty referral from primary care or general OB/GYN providers.
  • Reachable Patients (reachable_n): Patients located within a 60-minute spatial travel isochrone of an active URPS subspecialist.
  • Medicaid Eligible Patients (medicaid_eligible_n): Low-income patients enrolled in state Medicaid or Medicaid Managed Care plans.
  • Appointment Requests (appointment_requests_n): Total annual consultation attempts initiated by care-seeking patients (\(N_{\text{req}}\)).
  • Served Patient Encounters (served_patients_n / Served Encounters (M)): Total annual clinical encounters successfully delivered by available physician and delegated APP capacity (\(N_{\text{served}} = \min(N_{\text{req}}, \text{Capacity}_{\text{total}})\)).
  • Unmet / Delayed Demand (unserved_delayed_n / Unmet Demand (M)): Volume of patient appointment requests that could not be scheduled within 60 days due to capacity shortages (\(N_{\text{unmet}} = N_{\text{req}} - N_{\text{served}}\)).

Workforce Supply & Capacity Variables

  • Active Headcount (provider_headcount / supply_headcount): Total count of active, board-certified FPMRS/URPS subspecialty physicians practicing in the U.S.
  • Supplied Clinical FTE (supply_fte / supplied_fte): Total clinical Full-Time Equivalent capacity supplied by physicians and APPs, where 1.0 FTE equals 37.2 clinical patient-care hours per week.
  • Required Demand FTE (demand_fte / required_fte): Total physician clinical FTEs required to deliver benchmark care to 100% of care-seeking patients in year \(t\).
  • Net FTE Deficit (fte_gap / gap_fte): Difference between supplied clinical capacity and required demand (\(\text{Net Deficit} = \text{Supplied FTE} - \text{Required FTE}\)).
  • Adequacy Ratio (adequacy_ratio): Percentage of required clinical demand satisfied by available supply (\(\text{Adequacy Ratio} = \frac{\text{Supplied FTE}}{\text{Required FTE}} \times 100\%\)).
  • APP Delegation Efficiency (\(\delta_{\text{APP}}\)): Fractional physician FTE capacity unlocked per Advanced Practice Provider (NP/PA) working under physician supervision.
  • Latent Regional Adequacy (\(\theta_g\)): Bayesian inferred capacity score for county/HRR \(g\), bounded in \([0, 1]\), where \(1.0\) represents unconstrained baseline access and \(0.0\) represents complete access failure.

2. National Patient-Flow & Demand-Supply Conservation Ledger

The microsimulation enforces strict patient-flow conservation across every stage of the care cascade: \[\text{Prevalent Cases} \longrightarrow \text{Care Seeking} \longrightarrow \text{Appointment Requests} \longrightarrow \text{Served Encounters} + \text{Unmet/Delayed Demand}\]

Where: - \(\text{Prevalent Cases} = \sum_{g} \text{Pop}_g \times \text{Prevalence}_g\) - \(\text{Served Encounters} = \min(\text{Care Seeking}, \text{Supplied Capacity})\) - \(\text{Unmet Demand} = \max(0, \text{Care Seeking} - \text{Supplied Capacity})\)

3. National Workforce Capacity & APP Delegation Trajectories

Workforce supply is modeled dynamically accounting for entry, hours worked by age and sex, practice setting allocation, retirement hazards, and Advanced Practice Provider (APP) delegation: \[\text{Supplied FTE}_t = \sum_{i \in \text{Roster}_t} \text{FTE}_{i,t} + \delta_{\text{APP}} \cdot \text{APP FTE}_t\]

Where: - \(\text{Supplied FTE}_t\): Total clinical capacity available in year \(t\). - \(\text{FTE}_{i,t}\): Individual physician clinical FTE contribution (\(\text{Hours}_{i,t} / 37.2\)). - \(\delta_{\text{APP}}\): APP delegation efficiency factor (\(0.18 - 0.35\)). - \(\text{APP FTE}_t\): Advanced Practice Provider clinical volume.

4. National Empirical Evidence Lake Readiness & Parameter Provenance

The simulation integrates multiple authoritative external datasets into a unified DuckDB evidence lake: - CMS Medicare Part B Provider-Service Data: 2013–2024 (9.3M–10.1M rows annually) for CPT-specific procedure volume and setting mix. - NPPES Temporal Provider Registries: 2013–2024 fixed longitudinal credentials for FPMRS/URPS taxonomy verification. - CMS Doctors & Clinicians National Directory: Hospital affiliations and group practice structures. - UHC Transparency-in-Coverage Negotiated Rates: Commercial fee ratios and geographic price indices. - ACGME Case Logs: 2025 graduate procedural minimums (e.g., \(\ge 20\) sacral colpopexies, \(\ge 50\) incontinence procedures). - Epidemiological Anchors: Nygaard et al. (JAMA 2008) and Wu et al. (Obstet Gynecol 2014) for age-specific PFD prevalence curves; HRSA Health Workforce Simulation Model (HWMM) for population cell structures.

Clinical Practice Volume vs. ACGME Educational Minimums: ACGME case log requirements represent educational graduation minimums accumulated over a 3-year fellowship. In active post-fellowship clinical practice, full-time practicing Urogynecologists routinely perform 3 to 5 times these minimum volumes annually (e.g., 60–100+ sacral colpopexies/year, 150–250+ surgical procedures/year, and 1,500–2,500+ outpatient encounters/year). The microsimulation’s surgical productivity engine models true post-fellowship clinical throughput derived from CMS Part B annual provider claims rather than restricting provider capacity to fellowship educational thresholds.

5. Joint Bayesian Latent Adequacy (\(\theta_g\)) & Regional Sensitivity

🍽️ The Restaurant Reservation Analogy for Latent Access (\(\theta_g\))

Imagine trying to determine how easy it is to get a dinner table in a city (Healthcare Access Adequacy \(\theta_g\)). You cannot simply count the number of restaurants listed on Google Maps (Physician Headcount), because many listed numbers are disconnected, closed, don’t take your reservation app, or have 3-month waitlists!

To find the true, hidden Kitchen Throughput Capacity (\(\theta_g\)), you combine 4 clues:

  1. Calling Google Map Numbers (Listing Denominator): You dial 100 directory phone numbers. Disconnected lines, closed locations, and clinics not taking new patients fail immediately. Only 52.3% connect to a real reservation desk. This is Patient-Experienced Access.
  2. Walking Up to Open Tables (Eligible Denominator): If you bypass broken phone numbers and walk directly into an open, active clinic, 95.3% can seat you. This is Physical Clinic Capacity. (Relying only on open clinics overestimates real patient access by +43 percentage points!)
  3. Wait List Duration (Wait Time in Days): In high-capacity cities (\(\theta_g = 85\%\)), you wait 15 minutes (15 days for an appointment). In low-capacity cities (\(\theta_g = 20\%\)), you wait 3 hours (55+ days for an appointment!).
  4. Voucher Acceptance (Medicaid Acceptance Rate): Does the clinic accept public coverage vouchers? In low-access regions, only 20% accept Medicaid.

The Joint Bayesian Model combines all 4 clues into a single latent score \(\theta_g \in [0, 1]\) for every county.

Conceptual Framework & Measurement Equations

In urpssim, true access capacity is modeled as a latent regional parameter \(\theta_g \in [0, 1]\) for each geography/county \(g\):

\[\theta_g \sim \text{Beta}(\alpha, \beta), \quad \theta_g \in [0, 1]\]

The latent score \(\theta_g\) is inferred simultaneously from four observed empirical access indicators through measurement equations:

  1. Mystery Caller Listing Appointment Success (\(A_{\text{listing}, g}\)): \[A_{\text{listing}, g} \sim \text{Binomial}(N_g, \, 0.10 + 0.70 \cdot \theta_g)\]

  2. Confirmed Eligible Practice Appointment Success (\(A_{\text{eligible}, g}\)): \[A_{\text{eligible}, g} \sim \text{Binomial}(N_g, \, 0.60 + 0.38 \cdot \theta_g)\]

  3. New Patient Appointment Wait Time (\(W_g\), in days): \[W_g \sim \text{Normal}(60.0 - 45.0 \cdot \theta_g, \, \sigma_w^2)\]

  4. Medicaid Acceptance Rate (\(M_g\)): \[M_g \sim \text{Binomial}(N_g, \, 0.15 + 0.55 \cdot \theta_g)\]

Bayesian History Matching & Implausibility Metric

\[I(x) = \frac{|\mathrm{E}(f(x)) - z|}{\sqrt{\mathrm{V}(f(x)) + \sigma_{\text{obs}}^2 + \sigma_{\text{disc}}^2}}\]

6. Non-URPS Provider Ecosystem & Task-Sharing Cascade

Given the substantial demand volume generated by demographic aging, Urogynecologists (URPS specialists) do not provide all pelvic floor disorder care alone. Instead, care is absorbed across a multi-tiered provider ecosystem:

1. General Obstetrics & Gynecology (General OB/GYN)

  • Care Volume Absorbed: 45% – 50% of total clinical PFD volume.
  • Scope of Practice: Initial outpatient evaluations, basic pessary fittings, conservative pharmacotherapy, and straightforward primary surgical repairs (native-tissue anterior/posterior colporrhaphy, uncomplicated midurethral slings).

2. General Urology

  • Care Volume Absorbed: 20% – 25% of complex voiding dysfunction and lower urinary tract symptoms.
  • Scope of Practice: Male and female voiding dysfunction, sacral neuromodulation (SNM), neurogenic bladder, intravesical botulinum toxin injections, and upper tract urodynamic evaluation.

3. Primary Care (Family Medicine, Internal Medicine, Geriatrics)

  • Care Volume Absorbed: 15% – 20% of initial symptom presentations.
  • Scope of Practice: Routine urinary incontinence screening, initial lifestyle/dietary counseling, pelvic floor muscle exercise recommendations, and first-line Overactive Bladder (OAB) oral pharmacotherapy (anticholinergics / beta-3 adrenergic agonists) prior to specialty referral.

4. Advanced Practice Providers (NPs, PAs, WHNPs)

  • Care Volume Absorbed: 12% – 18% of ongoing outpatient encounters.
  • Scope of Practice: Routine pessary cleanings and maintenance, biofeedback coordination, post-operative symptom checks, and patient education under physician supervision.

5. Pelvic Floor Physical Therapists (PFPT)

  • Care Volume Absorbed: 100% of specialized non-surgical physical rehabilitation.
  • Scope of Practice: Targeted pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT), biofeedback, myofascial release, and neuromuscular re-education.

6. URPS Subspecialists (Urogynecologists / FPMRS)

  • Care Volume Absorbed: 10% – 15% of high-complexity subspecialty care.
  • Scope of Practice: Apical prolapse repairs (sacral colpopexy), complex mesh revisions/exposures, vesicovaginal/rectovaginal fistula repairs, recalcitrant OAB/UUI, and multi-compartment surgical failures.

7. Conclusions & Policy Implications

  • Fellowship Training Bottlenecks: Fellowship output (\(\sim 55–64\) graduates annually) is insufficient to offset impending physician retirements (peak retirement age cohort 60–68). Expanding ACGME fellowship allocations by +25% would reduce the 2035 FTE gap by 1,420 FTEs.
  • APP Delegation & Team-Based Care: Increasing APP delegation rates from 18% to 35% in outpatient care reduces unmet demand by 18.4%, demonstrating that multi-disciplinary care teams are critical to stabilizing access.
  • Primary Care & OB/GYN Task-Sharing: Formalizing clinical referral pathways and providing PFD management toolkits for primary care and general OB/GYN physicians prevents unnecessary subspecialty bottlenecking for routine low-complexity cases.
  • Medicaid Acceptance Gaps: Low Medicaid fee ratios severely constrain access for vulnerable populations. Model simulations show that increasing state Medicaid fee ratios to 90% of Medicare rates increases provider Medicaid acceptance from 42.1% to 68.5%.
